title: Mexico City: Rents Rose More Than Double Inflation in a Year
author: Mara Ximena Pérez and Nayelli Ramírez Bautista
content:
_This article by Mara Ximena Pérez and Nayelli Ramírez Bautista originally
appeared in the[August 10, 2026 edition of La
Jornada](https://www.jornada.com.mx/noticia/2026/08/10/capital/cdmx-
aumentaron-las-rentas-mas-del-doble-de-la-inflacion-en-un-ano), Mexico's
premier left-wing daily newspaper._

Nearly four months after the Mexico City Government announced an initiative to
incorporate into the city's Political Constitution measures that would limit
rent increases above inflation, expand social housing, and protect
neighborhood roots, rental prices maintain an upward trend. On this matter,
specialists warn of the need to contain their rising cost and the challenges
that applying these measures would entail.

In the past year alone, the median rental price rose 9.6 percent, compared
with inflation of 3.6 percent, while during the first half of 2026 it
accumulated an increase of 3.7 percent, according to the sales and rental
index of the real estate listings platform Inmuebles24, with data through
June.

The data show that a two-bedroom, 65-square-meter apartment costs on average
21,921 pesos per month in the capital, equivalent to almost 70 days of minimum
wage, while a three-bedroom, 100-square-meter one reaches 30,618 pesos, that
is, more than 97 days.

By borough, the highest rents are concentrated in Cuauhtémoc and Miguel
Hidalgo, with averages of 29,149 and 27,786 pesos per month; they are followed
by Cuajimalpa, Benito Juárez, and Álvaro Obregón, at around 21,000; Coyoacán
and Azcapotzalco, at 17,000 and 16,000, respectively; while Tlalpan, Gustavo
A. Madero, and Venustiano Carranza hover around 13,000 pesos.

## Gap by Neighborhood

The gap is also reflected among neighborhoods: Hipódromo Condesa records the
highest average rent, at 38,419 pesos per month, followed by Juárez and San
Rafael. In an intermediate range are Roma Sur, at 26,541, and Mixcoac, at
21,000; while the Pantitlán area sits at the lowest extreme, at 10,865 pesos,
3.5 times less than the first.

On this point, José Ignacio Martínez Cortés, coordinator of the Laboratory of
Analysis in Commerce, Economics, and Business at the UNAM Faculty of Political
and Social Sciences, noted that housing prices "were not cheap at all" to
begin with and that one of the consequences of the World Cup was the increase
in property costs in some areas, due to the improvements made in the city for
the event.

For this reason, he considered it necessary to apply measures to prevent
housing prices from continuing to rise, because current costs make it
difficult for people to afford even spaces of 50 or 70 square meters.

He said that a cap would be set using housing costs and inflation as a
parameter and that, on the other hand, that registry would also be created.
"And that's where, of course, many won't want to, because leasing is one thing
and paying taxes on it is another."

For his part, Alberto Pérez Naranjo, a civil and commercial lawyer, pointed
out that one of the main challenges of the proposal will be reconciling the
limit on rents with freedom of contract, since agreements between owners and
tenants stem from the will of both parties.

Regarding the creation of a specialized ombudsman's office to serve landlords
and tenants, he warned that there could be a duplication with the functions of
the Procuraduría Social.

In the end, he warned that difficulties in applying the reform could lead to
amparo lawsuits, "the moment they harm a private individual against their
guarantees and freedoms to contract."
